 Open health insurance enrollment drawing strong interest in Massachusetts
 Alison Kuznitz 
 8 hours ago 
 BOSTON (SHNS) – About three weeks into the 2027 open enrollment cycle, the head of the state’s health insurance marketplace expressed optimism Thursday about interest levels and a post-election landscape that could lead to the restoration of expired federal healthcare subsidies.
 Open enrollment at the Massachusetts Health Connector started Oct. 23, and Bay Staters who need insurance must enroll in a plan and make a payment by Dec. 23 to ensure their coverage starts on Jan. 1. After that deadline, eligible residents have until Jan. 23 to enroll in coverage that takes effect Feb. 1.
 “While it is still too early to draw conclusions or trends, we are heartened by the strong levels of engagement we’re seeing already from both current enrollees and new applicants,” Health Connector Executive Director Audrey Morse Gasteier said at a board meeting Thursday morning. “Our application systems, our customer service operations, and our navigator program are all operating at high capacity and performing exceptionally well.”
 Morse Gasteier said the Connector is keeping a “sharp focus” on the roughly 30,000 lawfully present noncitizens who are expected to lose eligibility for federal subsidies on Jan. 1 due to policy changes in the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
 “In tandem with that concerning focus, we are pulling out all the stops to keep as many people covered as possible and drive new enrollment among the eligible but unenrolled,” she said.
 The expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies in the Republican-controlled Congress last December created a chaotic open enrollment cycle. Connector officials and residents braced for huge premium spikes before Gov. Maura Healey said the state would  inject $250 million into heavily subsidized insurance plans offered by the Connector.
 Asked about the impact of that investment at a press conference last month, Morse Gasteier said, “We are seeing fewer losses in enrollment through the Massachusetts Health Connector than most of the rest of the country is seeing in like-to-like populations, and that’s because of how generous and protective and affordable the ConnectorCare program is for people who continue to qualify for it.”
 She said the $250 million investment reflects “how much more the state had to pour in and chose to pour in, even when the federal government pulled away the enhanced ACA premium tax credits.”
 The money came from the Commonwealth Care Trust Fund that receives employer contributions, transfers from the Health Safety Net Trust Fund, and penalty revenue from residents who don’t meet the state’s health insurance mandate.
 Democrats are set to control Congress in January, creating a new healthcare outlook after a wave of major eligibility and funding changes across Medicaid and ACA marketplaces. New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who’s favored to become the next House speaker, said last Wednesday that Democrats need to “ extend the Affordable Care Act tax credit s.”
 In a Sept. 1 memo sent to Jeffries and obtained by Politico, the House Democrats’ Cost of Living Healthcare Working Group mapped out a plan for the first 100 hours of the next Congress to “[r]everse H.R. 1’s Medicaid cuts and coverage restrictions and permanently restore enhanced ACA premium tax credits to prevent millions from losing coverage or facing higher premiums.”
 Morse Gasteier said voters across the U.S. last week sent a “clear and unequivocal message that healthcare affordability requires urgent action.”
 “We stand ready with the Massachusetts delegation and through the state marketplace network to partner with new congressional leadership and all our stakeholder partners committed to responding to the public’s urgent call for action,” Morse Gasteier said.
 The appetite for restoration of those tax credits may be growing, but congressional Democrats still face the prospect of a presidential veto as they contemplate policy platforms and consider ways to prevent sharp increases in the uninsured population due to new federal work requirements for some recipients of public health insurance benefits. 
 For the first year of the new Congress, the working group also called for Democrats to “commit to achieving universal coverage,” including by examining different single-payer and public-option models. The memo pointed to Medicare for All legislation co-sponsored by 114 House Democrats.
 Medicare for All platforms gained momentum on the campaign trail, including for Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed.
 Morse Gasteier said that “broader” policy talks on embracing a “new health coverage system have new life.”
 “We welcome those conversations and the energized focus on bold solutions for big problems,” she said.
 Medicare for All bills have failed to gain traction on Beacon Hill. At the Health Policy Commission’s annual cost trends hearing Tuesday, Commissioner Umesh Kurpad acknowledged the nationwide “sea change” that’s unfolding around Medicare for All and asked Attorney General Andrea Campbell for her perspective.
 Campbell said she sees it as an “opportunity” and said constituents must be educated about what major healthcare overhauls entail. She cited a recent experience with older residents on the North Shore who seemed misinformed about Medicare for All.
 “But I don’t know that they were in conversations with experts or policy decisionmakers who have done the work to really deeply talk about the pros and cons of any policy change and what that might mean,” Campbell said. “But it shouldn’t be off the table, along with other solutions that are out there too.”
 Medicare for All looks to create a tax-funded, single-payer healthcare system in the United States that ensures all Americans have insurance coverage. A KFF poll from September found that two-thirds of adults favor having a national health plan, which could be known as Medicare for All.
